activities.title: The mission
activities.instruction: Compose your response below, then submit to compare with the reference guide.

content.prompt:
You are working on a small frontend project.

The request is:

> “Add a compact status message to the profile page. Keep the existing behavior. Make the change easy for another engineer to review.”

You are given this starting state:

```text
main
  src/profile.js
  src/profile.html
  styles.css
```

Your task is not merely to make the text appear.

Your task is to **ship the change safely**.
guidelines: State your reasoning clearly in your own words or code.
Compare your response with the reference guide after submitting.

activities.title: Step 1 — Start from a known state

feedback.correct: Correct answer: A. Current branch and working-tree state.
feedback.incorrect: Correct answer: A. Current branch and working-tree state.

hints.text: What are you currently working on?
Think `git status` and the current branch.

content.title: Step 2 — Isolate the work
content.text:
Create a branch named something like:

```text
feature/profile-status
```

Why?

Because the status-message work should have its own history and be reviewable as one focused change.

activities.title: Step 3 — Make the smallest useful change

content.title: Step 3 — Make the smallest useful change
content.text:
The HTML already contains: ```html

Profile

``` Add a short status message: ```html

Profile

Your profile is up to date.

``` Do not refactor unrelated files.

content.question:
Before staging anything, inspect the state and the diff.

What are you looking for?

options.text: Whether the change matches the request and whether unrelated files changed.
Whether the branch name is funny.
Whether Git can guess your intent.
Whether the project has enough comments.

feedback.correct: Correct answer: A. Whether the change matches the request and whether unrelated files changed.
feedback.incorrect: Correct answer: A. Whether the change matches the request and whether unrelated files changed.

content.title: Step 5 — Stage deliberately
content.text:
Stage only the file that belongs to this feature.

Then inspect what is staged.

**Evidence target:** You should be able to point to the exact change that will become part of the commit.

content.title: Step 6 — Commit with meaning
content.text:
Create a focused commit with a message that tells the future reader what changed.

A reasonable message is:

```text
Add profile status message
```

Avoid:

```text
update
```

The commit message is part of the project's memory.

content.title: Step 7 — Publish the branch
content.text:
Push the branch to the shared remote.

Conceptually:

```text
local branch
     ↓
published branch
     ↓
pull request
```

activities.title: Step 8 — Write the pull request
activities.instruction: Compose your response below, then submit to compare with the reference guide.

content.prompt:
Use this structure:

```text
Problem
The profile page did not communicate the current profile status.

Change
Added a short status message below the profile heading.

Verify
Open the profile page and confirm the message appears without changing existing behavior.
```

content.question:
A teammate changed the same paragraph in their branch. The merge now reports a conflict. Their version says: ```html

Your profile is complete.

``` Your version says: ```html

Your profile is up to date.

``` Product wording says: > “Use the phrase ‘up to date’.” What should the final version contain?

options.text: The wording required by the product decision: “Your profile is up to date.”

feedback.correct: The correct resolution comes from intended behavior, not from winning the conflict mechanically.
feedback.incorrect: The correct resolution comes from intended behavior, not from winning the conflict mechanically.

content.title: Final engineering explanation
content.text:
Explain the entire workflow in your own words.

A strong answer should contain these ideas:

**1.** Start from a known repository state.

**2.** Create a focused branch.

**3.** Make only the requested change.

**4.** Inspect the diff.

**5.** Stage only what belongs to the change.

**6.** Commit with a clear message.

**7.** Push the branch.

**8.** Open a pull request with context and verification steps.

**9.** If a conflict appears, resolve it by understanding the intended final behavior.

**10.** Verify the resulting change before integration.

activities.title: Transfer challenge
activities.instruction: Compose your response below, then submit to compare with the reference guide.

content.prompt:
A teammate says:

> “I usually just edit files on main, and if something breaks I make another copy of the folder.”

Write a response that explains the engineering advantage of the Git workflow without insulting the teammate.


> “The main advantage is not that Git makes mistakes impossible. It gives us a structured history so we can see what changed, isolate work on branches, review a proposed change, and recover from mistakes with more information. Folder copies can preserve files, but they do not give us the same shared history or review workflow.”
guidelines: State your reasoning clearly in your own words or code.
Compare your response with the reference guide after submitting.

content.title: Module mastery gate
content.text:
You are ready to leave Module 2.5 when you can do these without copying the sequence:

**Explain:** What Git records and why history matters.

**Inspect:** Use state, diff, and history information to understand a change.

**Structure:** Use branches and focused commits to isolate work.

**Collaborate:** Explain local vs remote history and use a pull request as a review surface.

**Recover:** Identify whether a mistake is local or shared before choosing an undo strategy.

**Resolve:** Handle a simple merge conflict by intended behavior rather than by guesswork.

content.title: Forge takeaway & Lesson completion
takeaways: **Git is not a ritual. It is a safety system.**
> inspect → isolate → change → compare → record → share → review → integrate → verify
That is the beginning of professional engineering workflow.
nextSteps: Complete the mission and give the final engineering explanation in your own words. The mastery signal is not whether you memorized commands; it is whether you can choose the right Git action from the state of the work.
